title: NINE STATES

suspect.name: Daniel Shays
suspect.portrait_alt: A 1787 woodcut of two men in coats and hats, labeled as Daniel Shays and Job Shattuck, leaders of the Massachusetts uprising.
suspect.portrait_src: Daniel Shays and Job Shattuck, woodcut, 1787 · National Portrait Gallery, Smithsonian Institution · public domain (CC0)

intro: February 1787, Massachusetts. Daniel Shays has disappeared into the snow, and the state wants him found.
Twelve years ago he fought for American independence. Now he's a wanted man. Follow his trail and find out how.
Every place, date and document in this chase is real.

meter.label: States that have ratified
meter.line: Every stop is part of the case for a stronger government. Right on the first try: 2 states. Right after a hint: 1. Nine states, and the Constitution is ratified.

stops.story: Daniel Shays is a teenager in Massachusetts when Britain wins its war with France and is left with the bill.

clue.text: Start where the bill started. Open the Atlas: The Proclamation Line of 1763.

ask.prompt: What does the gray-blue color on the map stand for?
options: Land the Crown reserved for Native nations
Land the colonies could sell to settlers
Land France kept after the war
hints: Find the key on the map.
Who was the land set aside for?

question.stem: Based on Document 2, which historical circumstance led Britain to tax the colonies in 1765?
options: Britain owed a huge debt from a war fought to protect the colonies.
The colonists asked Parliament to help pay for their governments.
France demanded payment from Britain after the war.
The colonies had no governments of their own.
hints: Find the word “debt” in Document 2.
Who was the war fought to protect?
question.why: Whately says Britain carries a huge national debt, most of it from a war fought to protect the colonies. The debt is the circumstance; the tax came next. Keep an eye on debt. It follows Shays all the way to 1786.

stops.evidence: 1763–1765 · War debt leads Britain to tax the colonies · Document 2

stops.story: In April 1775, after the fighting at Lexington and Concord, Shays's militia company marches to Boston. That June he fights at Bunker Hill.

clue.text: Follow him to Boston. Open the Atlas: Boston, 1775.

ask.prompt: Boston was almost an island. How is it joined to the mainland?
options: By a thin strip of land called Boston Neck
By a long bridge to Cambridge
hints: Look for the narrowest strip of land on the map.
It's named after a part of the body.

question.stem: Paul Revere made Document 4 in 1770 and sold copies of it. What was the most likely purpose of this engraving?
options: To turn colonists against the British soldiers
To show that the soldiers fired in self-defense
To record the event exactly as it happened
To ask Parliament to end the tax on tea
hints: Look at how the soldiers and the crowd are drawn.
Who does the picture show as the victims?
question.why: Revere drew the soldiers in a neat line, firing into the crowd. The picture took a side, and that's why it spread. Five years later, militia from all over Massachusetts, Shays's company among them, marched to Boston.

stops.evidence: 1770 · Revere's picture turns colonists against the soldiers · Document 4

stops.story: Shays is made a captain in 1777 and fights at Saratoga. But the army can't pay him in full. He leaves the army in 1780, and, the story goes, he sells a sword the Marquis de Lafayette gave him to help pay his debts.

clue.text: Find what he was fighting for. Open the Threads map.

ask.prompt: Find the stop from July 1776. What is it called?
hints: Look at the stops dated 1776.
Read the line from “Remember the ladies” to the next stop.

question.stem: Document 8 says people have “certain rights that cannot be taken away.” Which principle from your Civic Principles card is this?
hints: Where do these rights come from, according to Document 8?
Rights you're born with have a name on your card.
question.why: Rights you're born with, that no government gives and no government can take away, are natural rights. Shays fought under those words. By 1780 he couldn't even get paid for it.

stops.evidence: 1776 · Rights no government can take away · Document 8

stops.story: Why wasn't Shays paid? Congress never had the power to tax. That weakness was written into their first plan of government, which took effect in 1781.

ask.prompt: Which article says how the national government gets its money?
hints: Look for the word “taxes.”
It's the article about the costs of war.

question.stem: Based on Document 11, why did the national government have trouble paying its soldiers?
options: Only the state legislatures could set and collect taxes.
Congress spent its money on a navy.
Each state had two votes in Congress.
The Articles let Congress tax only foreign trade.
hints: Who collects the taxes in Article VIII?
If Congress can't collect money, can it pay anyone?
question.why: Article VIII leaves the taxes to “the legislatures of the several states.” Congress could ask the states for money, but it couldn't collect any. No money meant no pay for soldiers like Shays.

stops.evidence: 1781 · Congress can't collect taxes, so it can't pay its soldiers · Document 11

stops.story: Back home, Massachusetts taxes its farmers hard, and the courts take farms for unpaid debts. In 1786, armed farmers close the courts. In January 1787, Shays and about 1,500 men march on the arsenal at Springfield and are driven off. In February, the state's army surprises them at Petersham in a snowstorm.

clue.text: Open the Threads map. Follow the line from the Articles of Confederation to the Constitution.

ask.prompt: What kind of connection is that line?
hints: Look at the tag on the line.
Did one help bring about the other?

question.stem: In November 1786, after farmers closed the courts, Washington writes about “these disorders” in Document 12. What did he think they showed?
options: The national government was too weak to keep order.
The farmers were secretly working for Britain.
Massachusetts needed a king of its own.
The states should leave the Union.
hints: Find the sentence with the word “weakness.”
Read his question that starts “If no power exists…”
question.why: Washington asks, “What stronger evidence can be given of the weakness of our governments than these disorders?” Shays' Rebellion scared the country's leaders into acting.

stops.evidence: 1786–1787 · Shays' Rebellion shows the government is too weak · Document 12
stops.nearMiss: You just missed him. Shays has escaped north, to Vermont.

stops.story: While Shays hides in Vermont, delegates from the states meet in Philadelphia that summer and write a new plan of government.

ask.prompt: Which section gives Congress the power to “lay and collect taxes”?
hints: “Lay” a tax means set a tax. Look for the word “taxes.”
It's the last section in the document.

question.stem: Which problem from the Articles of Confederation did Article I, Section 8 fix?
options: Citizens had no freedom of speech.
The Supreme Court had too much power.
hints: Think back to Article VIII at the 1781 stop.
What couldn't Congress do under the Articles?
question.why: Section 8 says Congress can “lay and collect taxes … to pay the debts.” A Congress that can collect money can pay its soldiers and its debts. Before, it could only ask the states. After, it could collect.

stops.evidence: 1787 · The new Congress can lay and collect taxes · Document 14

door.text: The Constitution goes to the states. It needs nine to ratify. In newspapers across the states, both sides are arguing.

question.stem: Hamilton (Document 13) and an Antifederalist (Document 16) disagree. What are they arguing about?
options: How much power the national government should have
Whether to declare independence from Britain
Whether to end the slave trade
Whether to go to war with France
hints: Hamilton says the states' failures stopped “all the wheels of the national government.”
The Antifederalist fears “unbounded” power.
question.why: Hamilton says the states' failures stopped “all the wheels of the national government.” The Antifederalist fears “undefined, unbounded and immense power.” It's the fight this whole unit is about: too weak, or too strong?

ratified: On June 21, 1788, New Hampshire becomes the ninth state. The Constitution is ratified. The new government starts work in 1789.
And Daniel Shays? He's pardoned that same year. The rebellion named for him helped push the country's leaders to write it.
door.short: Ratified anyway: in June 1788, New Hampshire became the ninth state. Your pair was {n} states short of nine. History didn't wait, but your case for it was weaker.
door.short_one: Ratified anyway: in June 1788, New Hampshire became the ninth state. Your pair was 1 state short of nine. History didn't wait, but your case for it was weaker.

acts.title: Act II · The new government's first tests, 1788–1825
intro: Pardoned in 1788, Daniel Shays is out of the fight. He later moves to western New York.
The new government isn't out of the fight. It can collect taxes now. The question is how far its power reaches.
Two more stops. No meter this time: just the trail.

stops.story: Washington warned the country about political parties in 1796. Two years later, with war with France feared, the party in power passes a law against criticizing the government.

clue.text: Open the Threads map. Follow the line from the Bill of Rights to the Sedition Act.

ask.prompt: The line's reason says the Sedition Act tests five words. Which ones?
hints: Read the line's one-line reason.
They're the first words of the First Amendment.

question.stem: Critics said the Sedition Act broke the First Amendment's promise of free speech and a free press. Which principle from your Civic Principles card is that?
hints: Look at what Section 2 of Document 19 makes a crime: writing, printing, saying.
Which principle covers freedoms like speech and the press?
question.why: Section 2 makes it a crime to write, print or say false and malicious things against the government. Critics said that broke the First Amendment's promise that Congress would make no law abridging freedom of speech or of the press. Many of the people charged were newspaper editors and printers on the other side.

stops.evidence: 1798 · The Sedition Act tests freedom of speech and the press · Document 19

stops.story: The Supreme Court, led by Chief Justice John Marshall, settles two big questions: who decides what the Constitution means (1803), and how far the national government's power reaches (1819).

clue.text: Open the Threads map. Follow the line from Marbury v. Madison to McCulloch v. Maryland.

ask.prompt: What kind of connection is that line?
hints: Look at the tag on the line.
Did the power the Court claimed in 1803 help bring about the 1819 ruling?

question.stem: Based on Document 21, how did McCulloch v. Maryland change the balance between the national government and the states?
options: A state could not tax or control the national government's lawful work.
A state could cancel any federal law it disliked.
Congress lost the power to create a national bank.
The Supreme Court gave up the power to review laws.
hints: Read the last sentence of Document 21.
Who wins when a state tries to tax the national bank?
question.why: Marshall wrote, “The power to tax involves the power to destroy.” If a state could tax the national bank, it could tax it out of existence, so the Court said no state may tax the bank's work. Under the Articles, Congress couldn't collect a tax. By 1819, a state couldn't even tax the national bank's work.

stops.evidence: 1819 · No state can tax or control the national government's lawful work · Document 21

final.prompt: Last question. From 1781 on, stop after stop was a fight over one thing: how much power the national government gets, and how much the states keep. Which principle from your Civic Principles card is that?
final.after: Federalism: Power is divided between the national government and the states. When they clash, valid federal law wins.

end.alt: Daniel Shays's gravestone in Livingston County, New York.
end.credit: Photo: Billmckern, Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0
lines: Daniel Shays died in Sparta, New York, in 1825, a poor man.
He lived his last years on a federal pension for his service in the Revolution. Think back to 1781: a government that can collect taxes can pay its old soldiers.
He's buried in Livingston County, New York, about 50 miles from this room.

reflection: Which stop did you get on the first try, and how?
Rebel or patriot: what would someone on the other side say?
What's one thing from today you'll use on the test tomorrow?
